blocks.text: Good news: most of the time you **do not have to write** these three modes. For a heap-owning type (`List`, `string`, `Box` and structs containing them), if you write no mode on the parameter the compiler **looks at the function body and detects the mode itself**:
If the body only **reads** the parameter → `read`; if it **changes** it → `lend`; if it **moves** it to another owner → `consume`.

None of the three functions has a mode written. `add` became `lend` because it changes the list, `total` became `read` because it only reads, and `wrap` became `consume` because it puts the list inside `Bag`. After `wrap(v)` the variable `v` can no longer be used; if you try, the compiler reports the error and also tells you **the mode it detected and why**.

With Copy types such as numbers and plain structs, if no mode is written the value is **copied** and cannot be changed inside the function; to change it in place you write `lend` out (`n: lend i32`). You can always write the mode yourself (for readability, or to pin the decision down).

blocks.prompt: Without writing any mode, write `keep(xs: List[i32]) -> Bag`: it puts the list inside a `Bag` (the compiler detects this as `consume`). In `main` call it with a 3-element list and print `b.items.len`.
blocks.hint: `return Bag{ items: xs }`; then `b = keep(v)` and `print(b.items.len)`.

blocks.q: You wrote no mode on a heap-owning `List` parameter and the body calls `xs.push(1)`. Which mode does the compiler detect?
blocks.why: The body changes the list, so the mode is `lend`; you do not have to write it.
